input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-140: Computer Science for AP Students. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: This accelerated course covers material from the first-year sequence of courses and provides the foundation for all subsequent Computer Science courses. The course stresses problem solving while covering modern software development techniques and introducing essential software tools. Topics include tree and graph structures, nested data structures, objects, classes, inheritance, interfaces, object-oriented collection class libraries for abstract data types (e.g. stacks, queues, maps, and trees), and static vs. dynamic data types. Concepts of object- oriented design are a large part of the course. Software qualities related to object orientation, namely cohesion, minimal coupling, modifiability, and extensibility, are all introduced in this course, as well as a few elementary object-oriented design patterns. Input and output streams, graphical user interfaces, and exception handling are covered. Note: Requires department permission for registration. Contact Hours: Lecture/Lab 6 It may be used to fulfill one of the following: GE: Elective, GE: Mathematical Perspective, NTID Math Processes, SMTL: Science/Math Literacy Typically Offered: Fall Every beat must be directly relevant to that catalog description. Prefer the RIT catalog source for scope claims. Use a supplemental source only when its cited claim teaches a named course topic; never use an unrelated source merely to fill a claim slot. Keep production directions exclusively in visualDirection and never say phrases such as 'on screen', 'show on screen', 'cut to', or 'camera' in narration. Regeneration revision 4: use ten distinct, specific beat titles and avoid repeating any title or section label.

Source excerpts:

[opendsa-programming-foundations]
Programming begins with precise problem statements, input and output examples, and algorithms written independently of syntax. Variables represent values and state, expressions compute values, and control structures select or repeat operations. Functions decompose a solution into named operations with parameters and results. Recursion solves a problem through smaller instances and requires a base case. Lists represent ordered sequences, stacks use last-in first-out access, queues use first-in first-out access, trees represent hierarchy, and graphs represent connected entities. Searching and sorting algorithms depend on representation and invariants. Correctness arguments, tests, tracing, and debugging compare intended behavior with observable results, including boundary and error cases.

[python-language-reference]
The Python language reference specifies lexical analysis, data model behavior, execution, expressions, statements, functions, classes, exceptions, and module import semantics. Python objects have identity, a type, and a value. Names are bound to objects within namespaces and scopes. Expressions produce values, while statements control execution and bindings. Exceptions interrupt normal control flow until a matching handler processes them or they propagate. The import system searches for modules and binds loaded modules into a namespace. Programs should be reasoned about through explicit state, control flow, data representation, contracts, tests, and observable behavior. Debugging separates syntax, runtime, and logical failures, while decomposition and abstraction reduce the number of interacting concerns.

The course stresses problem solving while covering modern software development techniques and introducing essential software tools. Topics include tree and graph structures, nested data structures, objects, classes, inheritance, interfaces, object-oriented collection class libraries for abstract data types (e.g. stacks, queues, maps, and trees), and static vs. dynamic data types. Concepts of object- oriented design are a large part of the course. Software qualities related to object orientation, namely cohesion, minimal coupling, modifiability, and extensibility, are all introduced in this course, as well as a few elementary object-oriented design patterns. Input and output streams, graphical user interfaces, and exception handling are covered. Note: Requires department permission for registration. beats.claim: Programming begins with precise problem statements, input and output examples, and algorithms written independently of syntax.
beats.example: A student defines a sorting problem by listing input arrays and expected sorted outputs before writing any code.
beats.title: Problem Statement and Algorithmic Foundations
beats.visualDirection: Display a split-screen: left side shows a textual problem statement with input/output examples; right side shows a flowchart of the algorithmic steps.

beats.claim: Lists represent ordered sequences, stacks use last-in first-out access, and queues use first-in first-out access.
beats.example: A stack of plates is added and removed only from the top, while a line of people waiting for a bus is processed from the front.
beats.title: Data Representation: Lists, Stacks, and Queues
beats.visualDirection: Animate three separate diagrams: a linear list with indices, a stack with arrows pointing only to the top element, and a queue with arrows entering at the tail and leaving at the head.

beats.claim: Trees represent hierarchy and graphs represent connected entities, forming the basis for nested data structures.
beats.example: A family tree illustrates hierarchical relationships, while a subway map illustrates a graph of connected stations.
beats.title: Hierarchical and Connected Structures
beats.visualDirection: Render a binary tree diagram with labeled nodes and edges, followed by a directed graph with multiple cycles and labeled vertices.

beats.claim: Objects have identity, a type, and a value; classes define these attributes and support inheritance to create new types.
beats.example: A 'Dog' class inherits from an 'Animal' class, gaining shared attributes like 'name' while adding specific ones like 'bark'.
beats.title: Objects, Classes, and Inheritance
beats.visualDirection: Show a UML class diagram with an 'Animal' superclass and a 'Dog' subclass, highlighting the inheritance arrow and instance attributes.

beats.claim: Cohesion measures how related the responsibilities of a module are, while minimal coupling ensures modules depend on few others.
beats.example: A 'PaymentProcessor' class has high cohesion because it handles only payment logic, and low coupling because it does not directly access database tables.
beats.title: Software Qualities: Cohesion and Coupling
beats.visualDirection: Present two side-by-side code snippets: one tightly coupled with multiple imports and direct variable access, and one loosely coupled using interfaces or abstract classes.

beats.claim: Object-oriented collection class libraries provide ready-made implementations for stacks, queues, maps, and trees.
beats.example: Using Python's collections module, a developer instantiates a deque as a stack or a defaultdict as a map without writing low-level logic.
beats.title: Abstract Data Types and Collection Libraries
beats.visualDirection: Display a table listing Python collection classes (e.g., list, deque, dict, defaultdict) with brief descriptions of their primary operations.

beats.claim: Exceptions interrupt normal control flow until a matching handler processes them or they propagate, allowing robust error management.
beats.example: A division-by-zero error is caught by a try/except block that logs the error and returns a default value instead of crashing.
beats.title: Exception Handling and Control Flow
beats.visualDirection: Animate a program execution trace where a normal flow is interrupted by an exception, jumps to a handler block, and then resumes.

beats.claim: Input and output streams provide the mechanisms for reading data from external sources and writing results to destinations.
beats.example: A program reads a text file using sys.stdin and writes formatted results to a log file using open('log.txt', 'w').
beats.title: Input and Output Streams
beats.visualDirection: Show a diagram with arrows labeled 'read' entering a buffer and 'write' exiting to a file icon, alongside code snippets for both operations.

beats.claim: Graphical user interfaces enable interactive software by combining visual elements with event-driven input handling.
beats.example: A simple GUI window displays a button; clicking the button triggers a function that updates a label on the screen.
beats.title: Graphical User Interfaces
beats.visualDirection: Render a mockup of a window with a button and a label, then highlight the button press event and the subsequent label update.

beats.claim: Correctness arguments, tests, tracing, and debugging compare intended behavior with observable results, including boundary and error cases.
beats.example: A developer writes unit tests for a sorting function, traces its execution on an empty list and a reversed list, and fixes a bug where the loop condition fails at the boundary.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Present a checklist graphic with four items: 'Write Tests', 'Trace Execution', 'Identify Boundary Cases', 'Debug and Verify', each accompanied by a small icon.

learningObjectives: Identify core data structures (lists, stacks, queues, trees, graphs) and their access patterns as defined in the course catalog.
Explain the role of objects, classes, and inheritance in achieving cohesion and minimal coupling within software systems.
Apply exception handling and input/output streams to manage runtime errors and user interaction in Python programs.
